Deployment

Source: vignettes/deployment.Rmd
deployment.Rmd

What you need to do around the app so that the protection the package provides works in practice. The package itself does not configure the Shiny server or the network.

HTTPS

Passwords and auto-login tokens travel between the browser and the server. Without HTTPS anyone who can see the traffic can intercept them.

  • The app must be served over https://. If TLS is terminated at nginx, Shiny itself can listen on 127.0.0.1 only.
  • The auto-login cookie is written with SameSite=Lax, and over HTTPS also with Secure (the browser will not send it over HTTP). Secure is set automatically when the page is opened over https://.
  • The app port must not be reachable from the outside network bypassing nginx (close it on the firewall).

nginx example

This is a template for whoever configures the proxy: substitute your own paths, addresses and certificates. The package’s automated tests do not check it. The key point is that Shiny uses websockets, and they must be passed through:

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name apps.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/apps.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/apps.key;

    location /myapp/ {
        proxy_pass         http://127.0.0.1:3838/;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header   Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header   Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_set_header   Host $host;
        proxy_set_header   X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
    }
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name apps.example.com;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

Brute-force protection and nginx

Lockout is counted per login, not per IP: behind nginx Shiny sees the proxy address, not the client’s. Consequences:

  • an attacker cannot bypass the lockout by changing address;
  • but they can deliberately lock someone else’s login (for lockout_minutes). An administrator removes such a lock in the user card, but you always need a spare administrator;
  • the global limit max_failed_logins_per_minute stops mass guessing across many logins.

If the app is reachable from the internet, additionally limit the request rate at the nginx level (limit_req).

First run

On an empty database, whoever opens the app first creates the administrator. Therefore:

  • create the administrator yourself right after deployment, while the app is not reachable by outsiders;
  • or create it in advance with a script: aa_create_first_admin(conn, "admin", password); the function works only on an empty table, and with concurrent requests exactly one administrator is created.

Weak passwords such as root/root after a migration will be found by aa_check_default_accounts(conn).

Configuration and secrets

  • Keep files with secrets (.Renviron, keys, service account files) out of the repository and in .gitignore. The package neither stores nor reads secrets.
  • A config.yaml with security settings contains no secrets and may be in git. It is better to pass database paths through environment variables.
  • The SQLite database file contains password hashes and token hashes. Only the app’s account should have access to it; do not put it in shared or synchronized folders.
  • If passwords or keys were ever in the git history, consider them compromised: change them; removing them from the history is not enough on its own.

Backups

  • Copy the database file while the app is not writing to it (at night, by stopping the service, or with SQLite tools: VACUUM INTO 'backup.db' from sqlite3).
  • Make a copy before updating the app or migrating the schema. aa_init_db() applies migrations in a single transaction and is safe on production databases, but the copy is needed in case of a bug in the app itself.
  • A copy with plaintext passwords (after aa_migrate_plaintext_passwords()) is dangerous: delete it after verification.

Password reset by email and nginx

If reset_enabled is on, the link in the email is built from reset_base_url. It must match what the user sees in the browser: the https:// scheme, the host name and the prefix under which the app is published in nginx. The package rejects addresses that do not start with https://, except for http://127.0.0.1 and http://localhost in local development, because a recovery token in an http:// link can be intercepted. If the address is wrong, the user will get a link that leads past the app.

  • The link token is single-use and lives for reset_ttl_minutes minutes, but while it is valid it is visible in the nginx access log ($request_uri). Do not hand logs to outsiders, and if needed write only the path without parameters to the log ($uri instead of $request_uri in log_format).
  • Emails are sent from the app session, so the process needs mail credentials (environment variables, not a file in the repository).
  • The limits reset_max_per_hour and reset_max_per_minute protect users from a flood of emails; additionally limit requests at the nginx level (limit_req).

Two-factor authentication: key and time

  • The totp_key encrypts the secrets in the database. Set it through a service environment variable (not in the repository and not in config.yaml next to the database) and store it separately from database backups: whoever has both the database and the key gets the secrets. If the key is lost or replaced, the secrets cannot be decrypted: users need to enable 2FA again, and an administrator resets it in the user card.
  • Server time must be synchronized (NTP): the code is bound to 30-second steps, and the allowed drift is configured with totp_window (1 step by default).
  • The QR code is built by the optional qrcode package; install it into the server library, otherwise users will only be shown the key for manual entry.

Updating the package and the schema

  • Update the package on the server through your usual deployment process (for example CI installing it into the shared library). The app picks up the new version when the service is restarted.
  • The database schema updates itself: aa_session_connection(..., prepare = TRUE) or aa_prepare_db(conn) at startup applies missing migrations and cleans up stale records. The schema version is shown by aa_schema_version(conn).
  • Migrations only add columns and tables, so the previous version of the app keeps working on an updated database.
  • After updating the package, read NEWS.md: it describes what changed.

Other databases

Besides SQLite (the default) the package works with MySQL / MariaDB (RMariaDB), PostgreSQL (RPostgres) and DuckDB (duckdb). The driver is installed separately, the app creates the connection, and aa_session_connection(connect = function() ...) closes it together with the session.

  • The schema is created and updated by the same migrations (aa_init_db(), aa_prepare_db()). In MySQL and PostgreSQL they run under a lock, so starting several app instances at the same time is safe. The database user needs the privileges CREATE, ALTER, INDEX, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
  • Create a separate schema (database) for the authentication tables: the package creates the tables users, auth_sessions, login_attempts, password_resets, totp_recovery, oauth_states and appauth_migrations.
  • In MySQL DDL cannot be rolled back: if a migration was interrupted, restart the app and the migrations will finish the missing parts.
  • DuckDB opens the file from a single process, so an app running in several R processes will not work.
  • Take the database password from environment variables, not from code.
  • Backups and privileges: for server databases they are set up with the database’s own tools (dumps, roles); password and token hashes are stored in the users and auth_sessions tables, so only the app’s account needs access to them.
  • Package tests against your own database: Rscript dev/run-tests-db.R mysql|postgres|duckdb|sqlite in the package sources (the test database must be empty: its tables are dropped).

Windows: database file locking

On Windows a SQLite file cannot be renamed or deleted while a connection to it is open. If the app opens a connection for every session and does not close it, it holds the file until the R process stops, and updating or copying the database fails.

  • Use aa_session_connection(): the connection is closed when the session ends.
  • If you open the connection yourself, close it: session$onSessionEnded(function() DBI::dbDisconnect(conn)).
  • Do not keep the database in a folder synchronized by a cloud drive: synchronization also locks the file.

Service and restarts

  • Run the app under a service manager (systemd, nssm and the like) from a dedicated account with access only to its own folders.
  • When the service restarts, open sessions are not lost: users with auto-login sign in via the cookie, the others enter their password again.
  • Stale login attempts and tokens are cleaned at startup (prepare = TRUE) and once an hour in aa_session_guard() while the app has signed-in users, so no separate job is needed for this.

Linux and Docker

The package does not call Windows commands and works on Linux. It needs the system library libsodium (for the sodium package) and the SQLite drivers that RSQLite installs. Keep the database file on a mounted volume, not inside the image, otherwise it will be lost when the container is recreated.

Pre-launch checklist

  • The app is available only over HTTPS, the Shiny port is closed from outside.
  • The first administrator was created by you, and a spare administrator exists.
  • aa_check_default_accounts() finds no weak passwords or plaintext passwords.
  • Secrets and the database are outside git; a database backup is set up and its restore has been tested.
  • Connections are closed together with the session.
  • Events (on_event) are written to a log that someone reads.
  • Roles and permissions have been checked under each role, and action handlers refuse without the permission.
  • If two-factor authentication is on: totp_key is set through an environment variable and stored separately from the database, server time is synchronized, administrators have 2FA enabled and recovery codes saved.
  • If password reset is on: reset_base_url opens in the browser, a test email arrives, and the link in it works only once.
